newsitem.title: USA: Getting what you pay for in a financial planner.
newsitem.headline: Getting what you pay for in a financial planner.

text.p: It's probably easier to pick a mutual fund than it is to find the right financial advisor, but that doesn't stop most Americans from seeking professional advice. We all just want someone to tell us what to do with our money.
Finding that special someone isn't getting much easier, despite industry and consumer moves that may be raising the level of financial advice.

Ten years ago, the biggest issue was finding a broker who wouldn't churn your accounts for excess commissions or an advisor who wouldn't push a bad partnership on you just because it kicked back 8 percent or better to him.

Now, focus on these practices has turned the public away from commissions. In a recent survey by Dalbar, a financial services publishing company, some 70 percent of Americans said they would rather pay a flat fee or an asset-based charge for advice. Younger investors, including baby boomers, eschew commissions in even greater numbers.

This public sentiment has nudged many commission-collectors in a new direction: They don't call themselves brokers anymore, but asset managers, financial advisors or planners. Fully one quarter of the advisory firms that trade for their clients through Charles Schwab are headed by people who used to be brokers.
Even the commission-earning brokers don't call themselves that anymore.

While this is generally a positive development for investors, it doesn't mean all of the advice out there is honest, or even competent. After all, a by-the-hour planner can pad his hours; an asset manager can overcharge for generic advice, and a top-dollar advisor can give bad advice.

A really crooked "fee only " financial planner can feed trades to his brokerage subsidiary and hit you with hourly fees and commissions. In some ways, the new payment mechanisms have driven the bad actors underground.
So face it: You can pick your own funds or you can hire someone to pick your funds for you. Here are some points to keep in mind if you are shopping for some help:

-- There's a lot of free and cheap generic advice out there. If you need some general rules about how to plan for retirement, how much to save, and where to put it, you may not need to go to a high-priced advisor. Check out the free offerings of some of the major no-load mutual fund companies. Most have decent planners that will suffice if your needs are of the everyday variety.

-- Credentials count. Certified Financial Planners (CFPs) and Personal Financial Specialists, who are CPAs (PRSs), must have experience and pass written exams, but either can depend on commissions. Chartered Life Underwriters (CLUs) and Chartered Financial Consultants (ChFCs) both come out of the insurance industry; a recent study by the International Association for Financial Planning shows their clients twice as likely to buy insurance for investment returns.

The National Association of Personal Financial Advisors screens SEC forms, requires certifications, experience and continuing education, and reviews financial plans to ensure their members are what they profess to be. They also are most likely to find members who are willing to do total financial plans, if what you want is a taxes-to-estate planning approach, instead of just a few funds.

-- Find an advisor to fit the question. If you have accumulated a nest egg that's too big to manage yourself, you might want an asset manager. Former brokers do very well at this; they have to really know a lot about investing before they can pass their Series 7 certification exam.
If you own a family business, have a sizeable estate or provide lifelong care of a disabled child, you should seek an accountant or attorney who has experience in these areas.

-- Seek the advice of someone who knows enough to have his or her own philosophy. Harold Evensky, a widely respected advisor from Coral Gables, Fla., sent his clients a four page, single spaced, small-type printed newsletter explaining his investment and money management philosophy. His clients know what to expect.

-- Expect to pay for quality, but don't pay too much. An asset management fee of 1 percent or more may make sense for the first round of fund-picking, but if you hold onto your investments for years, do you really need to keep paying and paying? And some advisors charge as much as 3 percent of assets per year. That can cover a lot of commissions, if you think about it.

-- Check credentials. Financial advisors must file detailed information with the Securities and Exchange Commission about how they make their money. Ask the planner for a copy of her ADV Form, Part II. If you are dealing with a broker, call the National Association of Securities Dealers at (800) 289-9999 to find out if the broker has ever been disciplined.

To check out non-registered financial advisors, call the National Financial Fraud Exchange at (800) 822-0416. This database will unearth links to criminal, civil, enforcement or administrative actions in the real estate, banking, securities, commodities and financial services industries.
